content: Vaccination is currently the only practical and effective method for preventing Japanese encephalitis. However, challenges such as production shortages, high costs, and issues related to licensure have hindered vaccination programs in many countries where the disease is prevalent. Additionally, concerns about the effectiveness and safety of vaccines have negatively influenced public acceptance and uptake. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness, safety (in terms of adverse events), and immunogenicity of vaccines used to prevent Japanese encephalitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in March 2007 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and BIOSIS. Reference lists were also reviewed, and attempts were made to contact corresponding authors and vaccine manufacturers. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), including cluster-RCTs, that compared Japanese encephalitis vaccines with placebo (either an inert agent or an unrelated vaccine), no intervention, or alternative Japanese encephalitis vaccines. Data were independently extracted by the authors, and the methodological quality of the studies was assessed. Dichotomous data were analyzed using risk ratios with a 95% confidence interval (CI), and vaccine efficacy was expressed as a percentage. A total of eight RCTs involving 358,750 participants were included in the analysis. These trials evaluated two commercially available vaccines and three pre-licensure vaccines. Two RCTs specifically assessed the efficacy of the inactivated Nakayama vaccine, which is commercially available. A two-dose schedule of this licensed vaccine provided significant protection of 95% (95% CI: 10% to 100%) for one year. In contrast, two doses of an unpurified precursor vaccine provided 81% protection (95% CI: 45% to 94%) in the first year and 59% protection (95% CI: 2% to 83%) in the second year. No serious adverse events were observed in these trials. Mild to moderate adverse events, such as injection site soreness, fever, headache, and nausea, were reported in less than 6% of children who received the inactivated vaccine, compared to 0.6% of unvaccinated controls. One cluster-RCT evaluated the live-attenuated SA14-14-2 vaccine, which is widely used in China, by comparing it to no intervention. Adverse events were minimal, with fever reported in 2.7% of vaccinated individuals compared to 3.1% of controls. Diarrhea and seizures were reported in 0.1% of both groups. Four smaller pre-licensure RCTs assessed a genetically engineered vaccine and two cell culture-derived inactivated vaccines. These trials demonstrated high levels of immunogenicity and relative safety for these newer vaccine candidates. The authors concluded that only one of the three currently used vaccines has been evaluated for efficacy in an RCT. While other RCTs have assessed the safety of these vaccines, they appear to cause only occasional mild or moderate adverse events. Further trials are necessary to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the currently used vaccines, particularly with regard to dose levels and vaccination schedules. Additionally, trials investigating several new vaccines are either planned or currently underway.
